Julius Caesar. On the Ides of March, March 15 in 44 BCE, Caesar was stabbed to death in Rome by a group of roughly sixty senators, including his trusted ally Marcus Brutus.

The murder happened in the Theatre of Pompey during a meeting of the Senate. Caesar was struck approximately twenty-three times by daggers wielded by the conspirators. His last words, traditionally rendered as "Et tu, Brute?" or "And you, Brutus?", capture his shock at Brutus's betrayal.

The conspirators feared Caesar's accumulation of power and his apparent moves toward kingship, which violated republican ideals. Caesar had recently been declared dictator for life, an unprecedented honor that alarmed the senatorial class. Brutus, despite his personal affection for Caesar, was persuaded by the conspiracy's leader, Gaius Cassius, to join the plot. The conspirators believed themselves to be saving the Republic from tyranny.

Yet contrary to their hopes, Caesar's death did not restore the Republic but triggered the Second Civil War. Mark Antony and Caesar's adopted heir Octavian, later known as Augustus, joined forces to hunt down Caesar's assassins. Brutus was defeated and committed suicide. Most of the conspirators were killed or exiled. Within a decade, Octavian became Rome's sole ruler and declared himself Augustus, founding the Roman Empire—the very thing the conspirators feared.

The assassination of Caesar embodies a tragic paradox: noble-minded men destroyed the very man they admired to save an ideal they believed he threatened. By killing Caesar to prevent monarchy, they ensured the collapse of the Republic and the rise of the Empire. The phrase "Ides of March" and the image of the betrayed leader stabbed by friends have resonated through Western literature and drama, most famously in Shakespeare's Julius Caesar, and through political rhetoric ever since. In history, it remains inseparable from the question of whether violence in defense of principle is ever justified.
